text: Define Channel<T> backpressure: bounded queue depth per channel, sender behaviour when the receiver is slow (block-as-Operation, fail, drop-by-policy), and expose queue depth via os inspect.
Publish interface design guidelines for IDL authors (naming, error taxonomy, async and stream patterns, capability-passing idioms) reviewed before the first Layer 2 interface freezes.
Decide that IDL compiler output is owned by the compiler's user with no copyleft obligation and encode this generated-code exception in every emitted file header.
rationale: Generated stubs land in every application, so unclear terms would contaminate the whole ecosystem.

text: License core platform interface definitions (IDL files and the ABI specification) under a permissive specification license with a royalty-free patent non-assert so third parties may reimplement them.
rationale: A decades-long ABI must be reimplementable by other kernels and runtimes without legal exposure.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide whether IDL-generated code is committed or generated at build time, and in either case add a CI check that generator output is deterministic and matches the checked-in interface definitions.
rationale: Typed IPC across a multi-repo or multi-language ecosystem breaks silently when generated stubs drift from their IDL.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Have the IDL compiler emit fuzz harnesses and structure-aware mutators for every interface and wire format it generates.
rationale: Typed IPC boundaries are the trust boundaries between components and each one must be fuzzed for free rather than by hand.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Run a measured IPC fast-path spike comparing shared ring buffers, register-carried small messages, seL4/LRPC-style direct scheduler handoff, and io_uring-style batched submission on identical hardware, and record results in an ADR before Channel<T> kernel semantics are fixed.
rationale: The baseline lists candidate techniques but the 1.0 ABI cannot freeze the channel primitive until one technique is chosen on measured numbers rather than intuition.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Measure same-core versus cross-core channel round-trip separately and decide whether the kernel offers synchronous 'call' semantics (time-slice donation to the callee) in addition to asynchronous send.
rationale: Call semantics change scheduler and ABI shape irreversibly, and cross-core cost often dominates real desktop IPC workloads.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the IDL (adopt WIT, adopt FIDL, adopt Cap'n Proto schema, or design new) using a written evaluation against ownership transfer, capability passing, versioning, streams and multi-language codegen.
rationale: The IDL is the language every platform interface is written in and switching after V1 would invalidate every generated binding.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Benchmark wire encodings (in-place zero-copy access vs compact encode/decode) including receiver-side validation cost, and decide the message representation.
rationale: Encoding cost is a fixed tax on every IPC message and validation cost is a security requirement that must be measured, not assumed.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Exercise the interface versioning scheme by evolving one real interface through three incompatible revisions in the V0 prototype before the scheme is frozen.
rationale: Versioning designs look correct on paper and fail on first real evolution; the failure must happen before commitments.

text: Define and implement Channel<T> as the fundamental typed IPC abstraction.
Define and implement Interface<T> as the fundamental typed service contract abstraction.
Kernel Core owns IPC (channel transport) as a native kernel responsibility.
Define Object<Channel<Message>>.
A Component declares typed Inputs<T> (receiving channel endpoints).
A Component declares typed Outputs<T> (sending channel endpoints).
The component ABI must be designed for long-term evolution; every interface definition carries an explicit evolution strategy.
Component ABI supports typed interfaces.
Component ABI supports interface versioning.
Component ABI supports optional methods.
Component ABI supports backwards-compatible schema evolution (adding fields without breaking old receivers).
Component ABI supports forwards-compatible extension (old senders understood by new receivers, unknown fields preserved).
Component ABI supports feature negotiation between endpoints.
Component ABI supports asynchronous methods.
Component ABI supports streams (multi-value results).
Component ABI supports futures (single deferred results).
Component ABI supports ownership transfer of capabilities and MemoryObjects in messages.
Component ABI supports cancellation of in-flight calls.
Component ABI defines failure semantics (error types, peer death, timeout).
Do not ship a typed IPC system without a simultaneously designed interface-evolution story; the IDL ADR must include evolution rules.
ADR: choose or design the IDL (new IDL vs WIT vs FIDL-derived) covering versioning, optional methods and extension.
Publish interface evolution guidelines for SDK authors, including compatibility test tooling that diffs two interface versions.
ADR: relationship between the native IDL and WIT (same language, bidirectional mapping, or independent).
IPC is one of the highest-priority performance subsystems; IPC benchmarks gate every milestone.
Implement Channel<T> as the primary IPC abstraction with typed message payloads (e.g. Channel<ImageDecodeRequest>).
Services expose typed interfaces declared in the IDL (e.g. interface ImageDecoder { async decode(Image) -> Bitmap; }).
Native IPC is not sockets.
Native IPC is not untyped byte[] payloads.
Native IPC does not use arbitrary per-service serialization formats.
Native IPC does not use hand-written protocols.
Native IPC does not duplicate schemas on both sides; the IDL is the single source.
IDL tooling generates the wire representation.
IDL tooling generates client and server stubs.
IDL tooling generates ownership semantics (which parameters move, borrow or share).
IDL tooling generates version negotiation code.
ADR: wire format for typed messages (fixed layout, self-describing, schema-indexed) and its zero-copy properties.
Implement the IDL compiler with Rust as the first target language.
Implement a minimal-copy fast path for small messages between sender and receiver.
Prototype shared ring buffers as a small-message transport and measure round-trip latency.
Prototype register transfer of small messages during a scheduler handoff and measure latency.
Prototype batched submission of messages and measure throughput gains.
Prototype lock-free queues for cross-core channel delivery and measure cross-core latency.
ADR: select the small-message fast path technique(s) from the prototyped options based on measurements.
Payload bytes must not move when avoidable; the IDL must make MemoryObject transfer the natural encoding for large data.
Resolve the size threshold and heuristics for inline small message vs MemoryObject transfer.
IDL code generation must emit tracing metadata for every typed interface method so IPC calls appear as semantic spans (cross-ref §14).
Failure and restart semantics must be part of every typed interface design; interfaces must define client behaviour on service loss (cross-ref IPC).
Decide the service naming and discovery mechanism that lets clients rebind by interface identity across restarts (kernel-held service registry vs user-space broker).
Channel<T> and semantic interfaces must not hard-code that both endpoints live in the same process or machine.
Do not make distributed computing a kernel concern.
Interface design must permit a same-component (in-process) transport.
Interface design must permit a same-machine cross-component transport (the default).
Interface design must permit a VM transport (native components in a KVM guest talking to host services).
Interface design must permit a remote-machine transport without changing application-level semantics unnecessarily.
Remote use of interfaces must surface latency to clients rather than hide it.
Remote use of interfaces must expose explicit failure semantics (disconnect, timeout, partial failure) (§32).
Decide the transport abstraction in IDL code generation (pluggable transports behind generated stubs) so remoting is added without regenerating interfaces (ADR).
Study Cap'n Proto RPC, Fuchsia FIDL/Overnet and Genode for capability semantics across transports before fixing the channel wire model.
Build a VM transport prototype (native guest component to host service over virtio) as the first non-local transport.
IDL code generation must target every supported SDK language (§14 tooling).
Native IPC must not require a userland serialization step for the common small-message case.
Native IPC must not require a data copy per hop for large payloads.
Native IPC must not require a userland deserialization step for the common small-message case.
Native IPC must deliver typed messages whose wire layout is generated from the interface definition (cross-ref §14).
Native IPC must support ownership transfer of MemoryObject capabilities inside a message (cross-ref §15, §16).
Native IPC must implement scheduler-aware handoff so a send to a waiting receiver switches directly to the receiver without a run-queue round trip.
Do not make everything distributed; distribution is not a kernel concern (cross-ref §43).
Study QNX synchronous message passing, resource managers and restartable services for IPC fast paths and recovery.
Create typed channels Channel<T> with IDL-generated message types.
Layer 2 core platform interfaces (compositor, storage, network, audio, package services) strongly versioned through the IDL.
Native Platform layer: Typed Interfaces.
Linux-derived kernel: IPC implementation for Channel<T> fast paths.
